meta.subtitle: Funded defense growth and a net-cash balance sheet, priced on earnings that are still mostly estimates and a cash turn that is not yet dated

analystSentiment.commentary:
Kratos is growing quickly while its shares have fallen. Second-quarter revenue grew strongly, and management raised its full-year 2026 revenue guidance in August; the income and growth sections carry the figures. The shares sit near the bottom of their 52-week range, and almost every analyst covering the stock rates it a Buy.

We rate the shares HOLD with a target range of $45–$64. The demand is real and the balance sheet is net cash, but the price rests on earnings that are mostly consensus estimates rather than reported results, and the company guides to another year of free-cash-flow use in 2026. We value the shares a year out on FY27E consensus EPS. Our weighted value sits above the price, but the Bear case sits far enough below it that the reward/risk test for a BUY fails. Two judgments carry the label together, the Base multiple and the depth of the Bear, and the valuation section argues both.

executiveSummary.companyOverview:
Kratos Defense & Security Solutions is a San Diego-based contractor whose main customer is the U.S. Department of Defense, which the 10-Q calls the Department of War. It reports two segments. Kratos Government Solutions provides microwave electronics, space and satellite communications, training and cyber, C5ISR and modular systems, turbine technologies, and defense and rocket support services. Unmanned Systems develops unmanned aerial, ground and maritime systems, including the Valkyrie jet drone.

The company says it makes internally funded investments to be first to market with hardware engineered up front for low-cost, high-volume production. It bids as prime contractor when it judges its probability of winning high and the investment within its comfort level, and teams with a large traditional system integrator otherwise. Management describes the growth areas as hypersonic and rocket systems, missiles, jet engines, and space and satellite communications.

The revenue split available here is by type, product and service, rather than by segment; the moat section reads it. By geography, the United States was 79.1% of FY25 revenue, Europe 5.8%, Asia Pacific 5.3% and the Middle East 4.9%. The fiscal year ends in late December; the latest 10-K covers the year ended December 28, 2025.

thesis.label: HOLD
thesis.body: Kratos is a beneficiary of the defense recapitalization the MD&A describes. Bookings run ahead of revenue, guidance went up in August, and a net-cash balance sheet lets the company fund its own build-out. The shares already price much of that. The earnings behind today's forward multiples are consensus estimates well above the GAAP line, and the company guides to using cash again in 2026 while it buys long-lead materials and builds plants. Its fixed-price exposure, which the risk section sets out, adds cost risk. Our scenarios put the weighted value above the price, with a Bear case deep enough that the reward does not cover the risk.

catalysts: FY2027 guidance, which management plans to give with the third-quarter report; the valuation section explains why it matters to the call.
The hypersonics ramp, which management calls a primary future growth driver; the growth section carries management's figures.
Jet-engine production for low-cost cruise missiles, with components on order for 2027 output; the growth section carries the volumes.
Appropriations turning into orders as the FY2027 request and the FY2026 supplemental move through Congress; the growth section carries the amounts.
A dated turn to positive free cash flow, which the guidance does not yet give.
risks: Valuation: the multiples rest on estimated earnings, so a slip in growth or margin compresses both; the valuation section carries the Bear case.
Cash use: the company guides to free-cash-flow use in 2026 and expects investment to continue into 2027.
Fixed-price cost pressure: inflation and labor costs fall on Kratos until long-term contracts are renegotiated.
Funding timing: shutdowns, continuing resolutions and appropriations delays can push out orders and payments.
The share-price fall: the shares sit near their 52-week low, for reasons the risk section cannot pin down.

income.note: Source: Bigdata.com company tearsheet (FMP); fiscal years ended late December.

financials.incomeCommentary:
Revenue rose from $0.8B in FY21 to $1.3B in FY25, with growth of +18.5% in the latest year, and June-quarter revenue grew +30.5% year over year to $458.8 million, of which 19.1% was organic. Profit has not followed. Gross margin slipped from 27.7% in FY21 to 22.1% in FY25 and was 22.0% over the trailing twelve months. Operating margin stayed between -0.3% and 3.4% across the five years and was 2.1% in FY25. FY25 net income was $22M and diluted EPS $0.13, after losses in FY21 through FY23.

In the June quarter the company reported an operating loss of $1.6 million, net income of $4.4 million and GAAP net income per share of $0.02; adjusted EPS was $0.21. The operating line absorbed $16.3 million of non-cash stock compensation, $13.6 million of company-funded research and development and $12.5 million of non-cash amortization. The quarter beat the company's own estimates on both lines: revenue came in above its $400 million-$410 million estimate, and adjusted EBITDA of $38.2 million was above the top of its estimated range.

The guidance widens the gap between adjusted and GAAP profit this year. FY26 operating income is guided to $16 million to $22 million on the revenue guidance the growth section gives, which implies a GAAP operating margin below FY25's, while the adjusted EBITDA margin is guided about 100 bps higher. Stock-based compensation is guided at $60 million to $64 million. The improvement on the page is sequential: third-quarter operating income is guided to $1 million to $4 million after the June quarter's loss. Management expects the 2027 adjusted EBITDA margin to rise by the same step again. Whether any of that reaches GAAP operating income in 2027 is the open question for the earnings the forward multiples price.

balance.note: Source: Bigdata.com company tearsheet (FMP); fiscal years ended late December.

financials.balanceCommentary:
The balance sheet is the strongest part of the case. At FY25 year-end, cash and short-term investments were $0.6B against total debt of $145.8M, for net debt of -$414.8M, a net cash position. The current ratio was 4.06 at year-end and 5.54 on a trailing basis, and trailing interest coverage was 5.2x. Total equity rose from $1.4B in FY24 to $2.0B in FY25, far more than the FY25 net income the income section shows; the source of the rest is not itemized here, so we draw no conclusion from it.

The net cash matters because the plan is capital-hungry. The MD&A lists facilities being built or expanded, from a hypersonic integration facility in Indiana to a planned small turbofan plant in Oklahoma and new microwave-electronics capacity in Israel, and the company is buying long-lead components ahead of awards. On the year-end figures, the cash covers the free-cash-flow use guided for 2026 several times over, so a delayed award slows the payback rather than threatening solvency. In our view the balance sheet sets a floor under solvency, not under the share price: the Bear case is a de-rating of a solvent company.

cashflow.note: Source: Bigdata.com company tearsheet (FMP); fiscal years ended late December.

financials.cashflowCommentary:
Free cash flow was negative in four of the last five years. In FY25 it was -$137.4M, a -10.2% margin and the weakest in the series, after capital expenditure of $95.3M; trailing FCF yield is -1.4%. In the June quarter operations used $11.0 million, which the company attributes primarily to working capital for the revenue growth through receivables, plus inventory for production ramps and investments in development initiatives. Free cash flow used was $18.9 million after $17.2 million of capital expenditure, and that figure is net of $9.3 million received for selling company-owned Valkyries.

The 2026 guidance keeps cash flowing out: operating cash flow of $30 million to $50 million, capital expenditure of $125 million to $135 million and a free-cash-flow use of $85 million to $105 million. Counting working-capital items and the Prometheus funding as well, total forecast investments are $250 million to $275 million, and the company expects these investments to continue at least into fiscal 2027. The MD&A says the component purchases for 3,000 jet engines address backlog as well as expected demand and potential awards, so part of the spend runs ahead of contracts. The strategy is coherent. The open question is when free cash flow turns positive, and no source in the pack gives a date.

valuation.multiplesCommentary:
On reported earnings the multiples say little: trailing P/E is 277.0x, EV/EBITDA 64.9x and price-to-sales 5.9x. The useful references are forward. The vendor labels its 56.8x P/E next-twelve-month, but it matches the price over FY26E consensus EPS of $0.84, so we read it as the current-year multiple. The shares trade at 42.2x FY27E EPS of $1.13. Peer multiples are pending a peer data source and there is no history of the stock's own multiple to compare, so the current-year multiple has no outside reference here.

Two features of the earnings base argue against paying the full current-year multiple a year out. Consensus EPS sits far above the GAAP results the income section shows, on a basis the vendor does not label. And the earnings are not yet cash: the company guides to free-cash-flow use in 2026. The case for the multiple holding is growth: consensus EPS rises by about a third from FY26E to FY27E on revenue reaching $2.2B, and management guides margins up again in 2027.

The Street sees more upside than we do: 22 Buys, 3 Holds and no Sells across 25 analysts, a consensus target of $98.15 (+106.1%), a median of $100.00 and a range of $74.00–$135.00. We use the lowest target as our Bull anchor. Reaching the consensus a year out would need FY27E EPS to carry a multiple far above today's current-year one, and only the share price earlier in the year, which the risk section describes, has reflected anything like it.

scenarios.name: Bull
scenarios.driver: The ramps arrive on management's trajectory. Hypersonics, engines and space carry FY27 EPS to the FY27E consensus of $1.13, the adjusted EBITDA margin steps up as guided, and free cash flow turns positive as investment tapers in 2027. With cash behind the earnings, the market pays more than today's current-year 56.8x, and the shares reach $74.00, the lowest published Street target.

scenarios.name: Base
scenarios.driver: Guidance is met and FY27 EPS reaches the FY27E consensus, but investment continues into 2027 and free cash flow is only starting to turn. A year out we value those earnings at 50x, a step below today's current-year multiple because the earnings are still not converting to cash.

scenarios.name: Bear
scenarios.driver: Appropriations slip again, and fixed-price cost pressure and the shekel hold margins down, so FY27 EPS stalls at the FY26E consensus of $0.84 while cash keeps flowing out. We value those earnings at 35x, well below today's current-year multiple: a market that has just watched a growth year slip, with free cash flow still negative, pays for the ramp resuming but not on schedule. A funded backlog and net cash argue for more; lost programs, or a need for new capital, which the 10-K flags, would argue for less.

valuation.scenarioCommentary:
We weight the Base at 50% and the Bull and Bear at 25% each. The weighted fair value is $54.10 (Bull $18.50, Base $28.25, Bear $7.35), an expected upside of +13.6% against a bear-case downside of -38.3%, for a reward/risk of 0.36×. The upside clears the +10.0% bar for a BUY, but the reward/risk falls short of the 0.50× a BUY needs, so the derived label is HOLD. The $45–$64 range brackets the Base.

The weights rest on the execution and funding history rather than on the multiples. For the Bull: the quarter's beat the income section describes, raised guidance, and bookings running ahead of revenue. Against it, the cash turn is undated, and the Bull needs a re-rating on top of delivery. For the Bear: the company itself expects contract funding to pick up after the late-2025 and early-2026 shutdown and continuing resolution, the FY2027 request is not enacted, and the fall the risk section describes is a market signal we cannot read. Against it, a mostly funded backlog and net cash cushion a slip. Neither tail has the stronger evidence, so they carry equal weight.

The call is close, and it rests on two judgments together: the Base multiple and the depth of the Bear. Holding today's current-year multiple on FY27E EPS in the Base derives BUY, and so does a Bear that pays today's FY27E multiple on the stalled earnings. A Bull at the Street's consensus target would also derive BUY, as would moving about ten points of weight from Bear to Bull; moving about five would not. We do not hold the Base multiple because that ignores the cash gap, and we do not adopt the consensus Bull because it needs a multiple nothing here supports; the Bear driver argues its own level. In the other direction, a Base that pays a year out only what the market pays today for FY27E leaves the label at HOLD, with the weighted value near the price. SELL would need the Base itself to fall well below the price.

segments.name: Product
segments.body: Product was 65.2% of FY25 revenue, $877.8M, with no margin or history given for the line. We assume, without a mapping from the company, that the hardware ramps management describes would land here: Spartan small turbojet engines, Valkyrie aircraft, and the 120 solid rocket motors procured for hypersonic and missile-defense work. If so, this line carries both the growth and the capacity spending. Any advantage here is a cost position in volume manufacturing, which Kratos pursues by designing for affordable mass production. Its value depends on winning the volume programs the plants are built for, and several of those are still opportunities rather than awards.

segments.name: Service
segments.body: Service was 34.8% of FY25 revenue, $469M. Government Solutions includes defense and rocket support services and training and cyber work, and management calls its satellite command-and-control and space domain awareness business the company's largest and says it is growing rapidly. How much of either counts as service revenue is not broken out. Because the split comes without history, margins or a business mapping, we draw no growth or margin conclusion from it and rely on the segment-level evidence in the growth section.

moatFactors.name: Programs and funded backlog
moatFactors.body: Most of Kratos's backlog is funded, and the FY2025 10-K says that if its unmanned products do not become established government programs, the company may not reach its anticipated growth, which makes program status the gate. An established program gives multi-year visibility. The same 10-K limits the point: backlog is an uncertain indicator, the company may not receive the full amounts, and government contracts can be delayed or cancelled without penalty.

moatFactors.name: Designed for affordable volume
moatFactors.body: Management's stated edge is being first to market with hardware engineered up front for low-cost mass production. On the August 4 call it described demand splitting between exquisite systems and low-cost ones, with Kratos supplying hardware to the primes and to new defense technology companies while also selling its own low-cost systems as a prime. A cost position has to be re-earned, though, and the 10-K says Kratos faces intense competition from competitors with greater resources.

moatFactors.name: Facilities and clearances
moatFactors.body: Classified program space, a hypersonic integration facility and engine plants require capital a new entrant would have to commit, and the 10-K names the facility security clearance as a prerequisite for classified work. The same assets are the source of the cash use and the fixed costs, and the MD&A says difficulty hiring and retaining skilled and cleared staff is adversely impacting the company's ability to execute.

moatFactors.name: Pricing power
moatFactors.body: The fixed-price exposure the risk section describes, together with the gross-margin decline the income section shows, means Kratos absorbs its own cost inflation for now. A supplier in that position does not yet have the pricing power a wide moat would need.

businessMoat.durability: We rate the moat narrow. Kratos is protected by a mostly funded backlog, by the facilities and clearances the moat factors describe, and by a volume-manufacturing position that fits what management says the department is buying. It lacks pricing power on fixed-price work, and its demand rests on appropriations that Congress sets each year. The moat widens if the engine, hypersonic and drone efforts become established programs with Kratos as an entrenched supplier. It narrows if budgets turn, or if margins stay thin as volumes rise. So far the franchise protects revenue but has not earned returns: operating margin stayed in low single digits across the five years shown.

points: Bookings lead revenue. Last-twelve-month bookings were $1.990 billion for a book-to-bill of 1.3 to 1. Backlog was $2.084 billion on June 28, 2026, of which $1.572 billion was funded, and the bid and proposal pipeline was $15.0 billion. Management guides third-quarter organic growth of 19% to 25% and fourth-quarter growth of 19% to 31%.

Government Solutions revenue was $379.7 million in the June quarter, up 22.0% organically, led by defense rocket support (+50.2%), turbine technologies (+43.3%) and microwave products (+29.5%); the Nomad and Orbit acquisitions contributed $40.2 million. Unmanned Systems grew 8.1% to $79.1 million, and management expects about 10% organic growth there in 2026 on recent awards including Valkyrie, with about 40 Valkyries a year planned from 2028.

Hypersonics: management puts this business at about $200 million of 2025 revenue, tracking to $400 million in 2026 and at least $700 million in 2027, and cites about $400 million of recently received hypersonic and other funding. It also cited a report that MACH-TB funding in the department's budget documents is about $7 billion over five years. These are management's figures from the August 4 call.

Engines: Kratos is placing initial component orders for 3,000 small turbojet engines to produce in 2027 and plans to order for an additional 5,000 for 2028, at an average selling price of about $50,000. Management sizes the low-cost cruise-missile opportunity at tens of thousands of engines. A turbofan plant in Oklahoma, pursued with GE Aerospace, targets larger missiles; management cited a report that the Air Force is looking to acquire over 11,000 JASSM and LRASM missiles over the next six or seven years.

Guidance: FY26 revenue of $1.750 to $1.810 billion with organic growth of about 18% to 23%. That is the press-release range; the call transcript's range starts a point higher, and the call also referred to a previously reported 15%-20%. We use the press release. Consensus has FY26E revenue at $1.8B (+33%).

Funding: the FY2027 request seeks $1.5 trillion and is expected to include significant funding for Golden Dome, space and satellite communications, unmanned systems, missiles and air defense, and the MD&A says the company believes it is well-positioned in areas the administration names as priorities. As of the August 10-Q, the request and an $88 billion FY2026 supplemental were subject to Congressional approval, and the MD&A says it is not assured that increases in funding will turn into more orders for Kratos.

management.leadership: According to the April 2026 proxy, Eric DeMarco is President and Chief Executive Officer and Deanna Lund is Executive Vice President and Chief Financial Officer. The proxy names three division presidents as the other named executive officers for 2025: Phillip Carrai (Space, Training & Cyber), Steven Fendley (Unmanned Systems) and Stacey Rock (Turbine Technologies). It reports that 2025 revenue grew from $1.136 billion to $1.347 billion with 16.6% organic growth, ahead of the $1.330 billion goal, and that adjusted EBITDA rose from $105.7 million to $119.9 million. That record, with the June-quarter beat the income section describes, gives the guidance some credibility. Our reservation is the size of the bet: management is asking holders to fund a multi-year build-out ahead of awards, and the return depends on those awards arriving on its timeline.
management.capitalAllocation: Capital goes into internally funded investment ahead of awards. Besides the capital expenditure the cash-flow section sets out, FY26 forecast investments include a $40 million-$45 million rocket-motor inventory build and $50 million to $55 million of funding for the Prometheus venture with RAFAEL. The list runs from a second production lot of 12 Valkyries to new microwave-electronics facilities in Israel. The company paid no dividends and bought back no stock in FY25. The allocation fits the opportunity management describes, and its test is conversion: plants built ahead of awards earn a return only if the awards come.
management.governance: The proxy filed April 2, 2026 describes nine directors, all standing for re-election, seven of them independent under Nasdaq rules; the CEO and CFO are the two who are not. An audit committee of independent directors reviews related-party transactions, and the company reported none requiring disclosure for fiscal 2025. There is one carve-out: for transactions with suppliers or customers in which an officer or director holds a controlling interest, the committee has delegated approval to the CEO, subject to quarterly ratification. For outside holders, that means the independent check on those deals comes after approval rather than before; the absence of disclosable related-party transactions in fiscal 2025 limits the practical concern for now. The compensation discussion describes 2025 goals spanning organic revenue growth, adjusted EBITDA, margin expansion and operating cash flow, but the excerpt omits the incentive weights and pay amounts, so we draw no conclusion on pay. Our view: governance is conventional apart from the delegated approval, which is worth watching in future proxies.
management.insiderOwnership: As of March 20, 2026, on 187,333,628 shares outstanding, the April 2026 proxy shows Eric DeMarco with 1,123,927 shares, less than one percent, of which 1,061,632 are held in trust with shared voting and investment power. All 17 directors and executive officers together hold 2,826,938 shares, 1.5%. The proxy also lists BlackRock, Inc. with 21,491,945 shares, 11.5%; the table draws partly on holders' Schedule 13D and 13G filings, so that holding may be dated earlier than March 20. The table lists a single class of common stock and no controlling holder, so outside holders carry the vote as well as the economics. Management's own stake is small, so its alignment with holders runs mainly through the pay plan the governance paragraph describes.

idiosyncratic: Valuation and an unexplained fall. The shares price consensus earnings the GAAP line has not shown, so a slip in the ramp would cut both the earnings and the multiple, which is our Bear case. The shares are $47.62, near the 52-week low of $43.09 and far below the $134.00 high. The price history shows them rising after the August 4 results and then giving that back through late August and early September. No source in the pack explains either move, and the latest headlines, from late June, report the shares rising, so we cannot tell whether the fall reflects valuation alone or news we do not have.

Cash use and funding. Investment is expected to continue into 2027, and the 10-K warns that Kratos may need additional capital to fund its growth and that financing may not be available on favorable terms. A longer investment phase than guided would draw down the net cash the balance-sheet section describes.

Fixed-price cost pressure. The April 2026 proxy says about 70% of contracts were fixed-price in 2025, and that Kratos cannot pass the related inflation on to customers until those long-term contracts are renegotiated. The MD&A says the difficulty of retaining skilled production staff has hurt operating margins, especially on longer-term firm fixed-price production contracts, and that supply-chain delays have pushed the company into larger advance purchases that use working capital.

The shekel and Israel. Management said on the August 4 call that adjusted EBITDA would have been $2.5 million higher in the quarter and $2.8 million higher over six months without the shekel's rise, because the Israeli microwave business is paid in dollars but pays its workforce and vendors in shekels. Kratos has over 700 employees in Israel, and the MD&A lists the conflicts in Iran and Israel among the risks to the industry and the company.

Program concentration and disclosure. The 10-K warns that losing or delaying a major customer, program or application could hurt results, and the growth case leans on a few areas: hypersonics, engines and space. Management said on the call that some drone work may not be reported until it ships, so outside holders cannot check part of the pipeline.
risks.systemic: The systemic exposure is the U.S. defense budget and how it is funded. The MD&A describes a large step-up: the One Big Beautiful Bill Act appropriated an additional $156 billion for defense and national security, and FY2026 national-security spending was expected at about $1 trillion. It also describes the friction: a government shutdown that began on February 1, 2026, continuing resolutions, debt-ceiling risk, and budget and deficit pressure. Any of these may delay, reduce or cancel funding for the programs Kratos is in or pursuing. The company expects contract funding to increase coming off the late-2025 and early-2026 shutdown and extended continuing resolution, which implies that episode held funding back. The MD&A adds that the effect of executive orders changing defense procurement policy cannot yet be known. Macro conditions add cost inflation and supply delays, including for electronics and SD cards drawn into AI data centers. In our view the risk is timing and mix more than demand disappearing, but timing is what moves a stock priced on next year's earnings.

body: **HOLD, target range $45–$64.** Kratos has the demand, the bookings and a net-cash balance sheet. The shares price earnings the growth should deliver but has not yet delivered, and the company is still spending cash to get there. Our weighted fair value of $54.10 is an expected upside of +13.6%, but with the Bear -38.3% below the price, a reward/risk of 0.36× falls short of the 0.50× a BUY needs. We stop well short of the Street's consensus for the reasons the valuation section gives.

The label rests on two judgments the valuation section argues: whether the market will still pay today's current-year multiple when FY27 becomes the current year, and how far a stalled year would de-rate the shares. We assume neither the held multiple nor a shallow Bear while the cash turn is undated.

We would move to BUY on FY2027 guidance, due with the third-quarter report, that supports valuing FY27E EPS at today's current-year multiple, meaning confirmed margin steps and a dated turn to positive free cash flow. On unchanged scenarios, a price at our target low would also derive BUY. We would move to SELL if FY27 earnings expectations fell to the FY26E level and the market paid only today's 42.2x FY27E multiple on them, which would put the Base well below the price.
